batchName: Late Republic: Cicero, Catiline and the Triumvirate (63-53 BCE) - Medium Batch 1
chapterName: Late Republic: Cicero, Catiline and the Triumvirate (63-53 BCE)

questions.question: Beyond crushing debts, what motive do modern historians add for Catiline's plot?
options: Wounded pride at failing to match his ancestors
A desire to free Italy's slaves
questions.explanation: Ancient writers blamed debts, while modern historians add wounded pride. The evidence suggests Catiline wanted a coup that would put him in charge, not a social revolution.
questions.sourceQuote: Modern historians add wounded pride, the shame of failing to match one's ancestors.

questions.question: Roughly how many senators flocked to Luca to curry favour in 56 BC?
questions.explanation: Some two hundred senators turned up at Luca, a sign of how much power the allies held. The deal there gave Pompey and Crassus another shared consulship.
questions.sourceQuote: Some two hundred senators flocked there to curry favour.

questions.question: Why did Cicero flee Rome in 58 BC?
options: A tribune's law banished anyone who executed a citizen without trial
He was convicted of bribery in the consular elections
The Senate stripped him of his honours
questions.explanation: A rabble-rousing tribune passed a law aimed squarely at Cicero's execution of the conspirators. Cicero fled to Greece and returned the following year.
questions.sourceQuote: In 58 BC a rabble-rousing tribune passed a law banishing anyone who had executed a citizen without trial.

questions.question: For roughly how long had none of Catiline's ancestors held the consulship?
questions.explanation: Catiline came from an ancient family, but none of his ancestors had been consul for some four centuries. Modern historians see this shame as a key motive.
questions.sourceQuote: None of his ancestors had held the consulship, Rome's top office, shared each year by two consuls (*consules*), for some four centuries.

questions.question: What word would the three allies probably have used for their secret pact?
questions.explanation: They would probably have called it amicitia, “friendship”, the normal Roman word for a political alliance. The label “triumvirate” came much later.
questions.sourceQuote: They would probably have called it simply friendship (*amicitia*), the normal Roman word for a political alliance.

questions.question: Why, in part, did Cicero publish his speeches against Catiline around 60 BC?
options: To prove Caesar was behind the plot
To defend himself against charges of killing citizens without trial
To win votes for a second consulship
To honour his fellow consul's victory
To teach rhetoric to young senators
questions.explanation: Publishing the speeches helped Cicero justify the executions. He also wrote a memoir and a poem celebrating his own consulship.
questions.sourceQuote: He published his speeches against Catiline around 60 BC, partly to defend himself against charges of killing citizens without trial.

questions.question: What did a satirist call the trio of Pompey, Crassus and Caesar?
questions.explanation: A satirist dubbed the trio a "three-headed monster". Cicero complained of "three men" holding kingly power, and one modern popular historian prefers "Gang of Three".
questions.sourceQuote: A satirist called the trio a "three-headed monster".

questions.question: Which Gallic tribe did the plotters try to recruit, only for its envoys to expose the scheme?
questions.explanation: A senior magistrate among the plotters approached the Allobroges, whose envoys revealed the scheme. Cicero then used them as double agents.
questions.sourceQuote: A senior magistrate among the plotters had tried to recruit the Allobroges, a Gallic tribe from what is now south-eastern France.

questions.question: Who actually commanded the government army that destroyed Catiline at Pistoria?
options: A deputy, after the consul claimed to be ill
Pompey, newly returned from the east
questions.explanation: The consul in charge claimed illness and handed command to a deputy. Catiline's army was destroyed and Catiline died fighting.
questions.sourceQuote: Their commander, Cicero's former fellow consul, claimed to be ill and left a deputy in command.

questions.question: Where had a former army officer taken up arms for the conspirators by 27 October 63 BC?
options: Near Faesulae, close to modern Florence
questions.explanation: A former army officer raised forces near Faesulae, a hill town in Etruria. Reports of armed men gathering there helped push the Senate to declare an emergency.
questions.sourceQuote: By 27 October a former army officer had taken up arms near Faesulae, a hill town near modern Florence.
